analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to sue police for misconduct and bans chokeholds, no-knock drug warrants, and racial profiling.
analysis.headline: The George Floyd Justice in Policing Act of 2024 died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or a vote, after being introduced with 10 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it much easier to sue police officers and departments for misconduct, create a public national registry of officer misconduct, ban chokeholds and no-knock drug warrants for federal officers, ban racial profiling, and require detailed reporting of use-of-force data. It would push states to adopt similar rules by tying federal policing grants to compliance. It was introduced in the Senate in August 2024, referred to the Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who suffer police misconduct — and their families — would gain a practical path to sue officers and departments, since qualified immunity would no longer shield local and federal law enforcement officers and the federal criminal standard for rights violations would drop from "willfully" to "knowingly or recklessly" [S2]. Communities of color, who bear the brunt of stops and use of force, would gain a federal ban on racial profiling with a private right to sue, public databases of officer misconduct and use-of-force data, a federal ban on chokeholds and no-knock drug warrants, and grant money conditioned on departments adopting anti-profiling and de-escalation policies [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Ends qualified immunity as a defense for local and federal law enforcement officers in civil rights lawsuits, so victims of misconduct can recover damages even when the underlying right was not clearly established in prior cases

Lowers the federal criminal standard for depriving someone of their rights from 'willfully' to 'knowingly or recklessly' and lets prosecutors bring a death charge when an officer's act was a substantial factor in the death

Creates a public national registry of officer misconduct and decertification records, and bars federal grant money to states and cities that fail to report misconduct or check the registry before hiring officers

Bans federal no-knock warrants in drug cases and conditions COPS grant funds on states banning them too; similarly bans chokeholds and carotid holds for federal officers and ties Byrne and COPS funds to state bans

Restricts federal officers to using deadly force only as a last resort when alternatives are exhausted, requires de-escalation training, and creates a duty to intervene when another officer uses excessive force

Bans racial profiling by all law enforcement, gives individuals a private right to sue over it, and requires data collection on stops and searches broken down by race, with grant money withheld from states that fail to comply

Requires body cameras and in-car video for federal law enforcement, audits of use-of-force reporting, and criminalizes officers engaging in sexual acts with people under color of law, closing the so-called consent loophole

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the main costs would fall on law enforcement agencies: officers would lose qualified immunity as a shield in civil suits and face an easier-to-prove federal criminal standard, departments would have to build misconduct-reporting systems and adopt use-of-force, chokehold, no-knock, and racial-profiling rules to keep federal grant money, and governments would bear the cost of new lawsuits and settlements. Federal taxpayers would also fund roughly $1 billion in authorized grants for state-level independent investigations and pattern-and-practice probes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Police departments and governments facing suits

drawbacks.text: The bill relies heavily on grant conditions: penalties fall only on states and agencies that accept federal Byrne or COPS money, and enforcement is left to the Attorney General's discretion, so agencies willing to forgo funds could escape most requirements

It authorizes substantial new spending, including $750 million for independent investigation grants and $100 million per year for pattern-and-practice investigation grants, on top of existing federal policing funds

Police departments argue that eliminating qualified immunity and lowering the criminal intent standard would expose individual officers to personal liability and make them hesitant to act decisively in dangerous situations, and that resulting lawsuit settlements would fall on taxpayers

Some use-of-force rules, such as requiring officers to exhaust 'reasonable alternatives' before deadly force, would apply only to federal officers and could put federal agents at greater risk in fast-moving violent encounters

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver real, enforceable gains for people harmed by police misconduct — a path to sue without qualified immunity, a public misconduct registry, and restrictions on chokeholds, no-knock warrants, and racial profiling. The costs are real but smaller: about $1 billion in new authorized grant spending, potential settlement and liability costs for governments, and a grant-condition structure that lets non-compliant agencies opt out by declining federal funds. The most contested change — ending qualified immunity — is also the one police unions have fought hardest, and it never received a public vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until Congress ended, never getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on August 1, 2024, in the final months of the 118th Congress
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced
The committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, and no vote appear in the action history
It had 10 cosponsors, all Senate Democrats, and no Republican support
A near-identical version passed the House in 2021 during the previous Congress but never became law; this reintroduction was an attempt to revive it

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies and police unions came out ahead: qualified immunity remains intact, chokeholds, no-knock drug warrants, and racial profiling remain governed by state rules and department policies, and no misconduct reporting requirements were created. People seeking police accountability gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police departments and unions, avoided new rules

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, his latest attempt after earlier versions died in prior Congresses

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled

against.name: Police unions
against.role: Police labor unions, including the Fraternal Order of Police
against.what_they_did: Opposed earlier versions of this same bill, particularly its qualified-immunity changes, during the 117th Congress

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Senate Democrat and no Republican supported it; the bill never got any action after referral, so no one ever had to vote on it.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies and police unions
industries.note: The bill would strip qualified immunity as a defense in civil suits, ease the federal criminal standard for violating civil rights, mandate misconduct reporting, and restrict use of force. In earlier Congresses, police unions opposed these changes, and no version has advanced.

States and cities would face new conditions on federal policing grants, including misconduct reporting, anti-profiling policies, and bans on chokeholds and no-knock drug warrants, with grant money cut for noncompliance. Some would receive new grants for independent investigations and training.
